# Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman is a pioneering computer scientist and activist best known as the founder of the Free Software Movement and the GNU Project. Born in New York City in 1953, he began his career at Harvard University and later worked as a researcher at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, where he developed early computer systems and became a prominent figure in the hacker community. In 1983, Stallman announced the GNU Project with the goal of creating a completely free operating system compatible with Unix, driven by a philosophy that software users should have the freedom to share, study, and modify the programs they use. He established the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 to support this movement and introduced the concept of "copyleft" through the GNU General Public License (GPL) to legally protect these freedoms against proprietary restrictions.
Stallman is a staunch advocate for software freedom, often using the term "free software" to distinguish it from "open-source software," arguing that the former emphasizes the moral and political value of user liberty rather than just the development model. He has been a vocal critic of digital rights management, restrictive licensing, and the concept of intellectual property, proposing alternatives such as a reduced copyright term and tax-based author support. Beyond his technical work, Stallman has engaged in global activism, influencing governments in India and Ecuador to adopt free software in public institutions and participating in protests against proprietary technologies. Despite facing significant personal controversy regarding his past comments on Jeffrey Epstein and Marvin Minsky, he remains a central figure in the free software community, having returned to lead the FSF in 2021.
